def: "Not-two." The view that ultimate reality is one, and that the individual self and that reality are not separate.
The true Self, beneath body and mind.
The single reality behind everything, in the Upanishads and Vedanta.
Self-inquiry: looking into who or what the "I" really is. Ramana Maharshi's core practice.
Devotion; love of God as a path to liberation.
Knowledge, specifically direct knowledge of reality rather than information.
Silence, both as a practice and as a form of teaching.
Shiva as the silent teacher, seated under a banyan tree, instructing old sages without words.
Spiritual teacher; literally "heavy" or "weighty."
An unbroken chain of teachers and disciples; a lineage.
A tradition or school carried by a lineage, with its own texts and practices.
Initiation; the formal entry into a lineage.
Formal renunciation; becoming a monk.
"Company of truth": gathering with a teacher or fellow seekers.
Seeing and being seen by a holy person or deity; also the word for a school of philosophy.
Deep meditative absorption; also the tomb-shrine of a saint.
Someone liberated while still living in a body.
A latent tendency or habit of mind carried forward from past experience.
The "I-maker": the sense of being a separate individual.
A family of traditions that treat the body, energy and ritual as means of liberation rather than obstacles.
Spiritual energy said to lie coiled at the base of the spine.
Transmission of spiritual energy from teacher to disciple.
The 63 Tamil saints devoted to Shiva, whose lives are told in the Periya Puranam.
Philosophical texts closing the Vedas; the source of Vedanta.
"End of the Vedas": the schools of philosophy built on the Upanishads.
Modern reinterpretation of Vedanta (Vivekananda and after) presenting it as universal, experiential and compatible with science.
Western satsang movement, largely descended from Papaji, that teaches non-duality with little or no traditional practice.
Poet-saints of north India (Kabir, Ravidas and others) who worshipped a formless God and rejected caste and ritual.
A Sufi master or saint.
Malayalam for core, embryo or mould; Narayana Guru's word for the one source from which knower and known both arise.
Malayalam for knowledge or awareness; in Narayana Guru, the one consciousness that appears as knower, known and knowing.
Birth group: both 'species' and 'caste'. Narayana Guru argued that humans are one jati because they share one form and one way of birth.
A wandering ascetic who has dropped social and ritual rules.
A course of spiritual discipline undertaken to reach a particular realization.
An emotional attitude toward God, such as servant, child, parent or lover, cultivated in devotional practice.
Absorption without any object or thought; in Advaita, the state in which only Brahman remains.
Discernment; in Ramakrishna's usage, a fuller realization after Advaita absorption that sees the one reality as both personal and impersonal and present in everything.
The dark goddess of Bengali Shakta worship, addressed by devotees as Mother; for Ramakrishna, God's power active in the world.
"Woman and gold": Ramakrishna's phrase for lust and greed as the chief attachments that keep a seeker from God.
Vivekananda's name for Advaita applied to everyday life: since the one Self is in everyone, serving others, especially the poor, is worship.
The path of work done without attachment to its results, one of Vivekananda's four yogas.
The path of meditation and mental control based on Patanjali's Yoga Sutras; also the title of Vivekananda's 1896 book.
Pronounced 'mutt'. A Hindu monastery; the Ramakrishna Math is the monastic order founded by Vivekananda.
A wandering monk with no fixed home.
Yogic breath control: deliberate patterns of breathing in, holding and breathing out.
The cyclic breathing sequence taught by Sri Sri Ravi Shankar in Art of Living courses.
"Skull-shining": a breathing practice of short, forceful exhalations driven by the belly.
Arrangement or placing in order; in Krishnamacharya's usage, a counted sequence of movements linked to the breath.
Recognition; the Kashmiri Shaiva school holding that liberation is recognising one's own nature as Shiva.
Threefold; Abhinavagupta's school of Kashmir Shaivism, named for its three goddesses and its triad of Shiva, Shakti and the individual.
Grace; in Kashmir Shaivism, the fifth of Shiva's five acts, by which he reveals his own nature.
The society of worshippers of Brahman, founded by Rammohan Roy in 1828 as the Brahmo Sabha; congregational worship of one formless God, without images.
A widow's self-immolation on her husband's funeral pyre, and the woman who does it; prohibited in Bengal on 4 December 1829.
Hymns to the formless Brahman sung in Brahmo worship; Rammohan wrote many of the first ones.
The oneness of God, the central doctrine of Islamic theology.
'Collection.' The four core collections of Vedic hymns and formulas: Rig, Yajur, Sama and Atharva.
A formal public debate on the meaning of scripture between learned opponents, often before a ruler or assembly.
Dayananda's doctrine of three eternal realities: God, individual souls and primal matter (prakriti).
Worship of God through a consecrated image.
'Of the rishis.' Texts held to come from the ancient seers, as against later works by ordinary authors (anarsha).
A fire offering of ghee and fragrant materials with Vedic chanting; also called agnihotra or homa.
An ancient rule allowing a widow or childless wife to have children by an appointed man.
'Purification.' An Arya Samaj rite and campaign to bring converts to other religions into Hinduism.
Title of the heads of monasteries that trace their line to Adi Shankara; a celibate monk chosen and initiated by his predecessor.
The classical scheme of four social classes (varna) and four stages of life (ashrama), each with its own duties.
Brahmin households following the smriti law books and Vedic rites, worshipping five deities, and usually aligned with Shankara's Advaita.
A 'victory journey': the traditional touring circuit of a Shankaracharya through the country.
"Play." The activity of God, done for its own sake with no need behind it.
A sacred fire kept burning by an ascetic.
Sacred ash from Shirdi Sai Baba's fire, given to visitors as blessing and medicine.
Faith and patience, the two inner offerings Shirdi Sai Baba asked of devotees.
Repeating a mantra or a name of God, aloud or silently, often counted on a rosary.
The fourth: in the Mandukya Upanishad, the consciousness underlying waking, dreaming and dreamless sleep.
The Radhasoami practice of joining the attention (surat) to an inner current of sound (shabd) and following it upward.
Gandhi's word for firmness in truth: nonviolent resistance in which the resister accepts suffering instead of inflicting it.
Nonviolence; not harming living beings in deed, word or thought.
Celibacy; for Gandhi, control of all the senses in thought, word and deed.
Non-attachment, especially to the fruits of one's actions, as taught in the Bhagavad Gita.
The person of steady wisdom described in the second chapter of the Bhagavad Gita.
Sri Aurobindo's name (purna yoga) for a yoga that combines the paths of works, knowledge, devotion and self-perfection and aims to transform the whole of life, not only to liberate the individual.
In Sri Aurobindo's teaching, a truth-consciousness above mind that knows by identity and holds the One and the many together; the next principle he expected evolution to bring out.
In Sri Aurobindo's map, the highest plane below the Supermind: vast and luminous, the plane of the cosmic gods, but still dividing truth into separate aspects.
In Sri Aurobindo's cosmology, the descent and self-concealment of Spirit in matter, which makes evolution possible: what evolves was first involved.
In Sri Aurobindo's teaching, the evolving soul behind the personality (chaitya purusha), which grows from life to life and can guide mind, feeling and body from within.
Krishnamurti's phrase for watching thoughts, feelings and reactions as they arise without condemning, approving or trying to change them.

A nineteenth-century movement founded by Helena Blavatsky and Henry Steel Olcott that blended Western esotericism with Hindu and Buddhist ideas and taught that all religions share a hidden core of wisdom.
In the Brahmo Samaj, the minister who leads congregational worship; more widely, a teacher.
The 'original' Brahmo Samaj, Debendranath Tagore's body after Keshab Chandra Sen's group left in 1865-66.
The New Dispensation, Keshab Chandra Sen's church (1880 or 1881), which treated all religions as parts of one continuing revelation.
The Society of Truth-Seekers, founded by Jotirao Phule in Poona in 1873 against caste and priestly mediation.
Phule's name for God: the Creator, worshipped directly by everyone without a priest.
A valid means of knowledge, such as perception, inference or scripture.
Offering of knowledge: Chinmayananda's name for a public lecture series on a Vedanta text.
In Advaita, the power or appearance by which the one reality seems to be a world of many things.
Selfhood or individuality; for Iqbal, the self each person must build and strengthen through love and action.
In Sufism, the passing away of the self into God.
Independent reasoning on questions of Islamic law.
Tagore's god of his own life, a presence that shapes the poet's life from within.
A wandering singer of rural Bengal who seeks the divine Man of the Heart within the body.
Self-rule; K. C. Bhattacharyya applied it to freedom of thought.
A channel of the subtle body; ida (left), pingala (right) and sushumna (central) in kundalini yoga.

In Lahiri Mahasaya's line, a set of breathing and concentration techniques, moving breath and attention along the spine, given by initiation in graded stages. Patanjali uses the same name for a discipline of austerity, study and devotion.
A hatha yoga practice in which the tongue is turned back and up behind the soft palate; part of Kriya Yoga in Lahiri's line.
Literally 'unchanging'; in Kriya Yoga, the point between the eyebrows where attention rests and the still awareness experienced there.
A householder: someone living with a family and an occupation, as opposed to a renunciant monk.
One of the four ages of the Hindu cycle of time: Satya, Treta, Dvapara and Kali. Tradition gives Kali Yuga 432,000 years; Sri Yukteswar proposed a 24,000-year cycle.
A yoga posture. In modern classes, one of the many named poses, such as the triangle or the headstand.
The branch of yoga that works through postures, breath control and cleansing practices, described in medieval texts such as the Hatha Yoga Pradipika.
A hatha yoga cleansing practice in which the abdominal muscles are isolated and rolled. Kuvalayananda's first published experiment was an X-ray study of it.
A traditional south Indian rejuvenation practice of breathing, diet and exercise, said to slow the body's decline. Vethathiri taught his own version.
In Tamil tradition, an adept credited with yoga techniques and with a system of medicine that also bears the name Siddha.
Literally supreme swan; a title for a monk of the highest spiritual attainment. Sri Yukteswar gave it to Yogananda in 1935.
Great samadhi; devotees' term for an accomplished yogi's death, understood as a conscious final exit from the body.
Yogananda's breath-watching concentration technique: the breath is silently paired with hong on the inhalation and sau on the exhalation until mind and breath grow calm.
Yogananda's early name for his system of tense-and-relax energization exercises and meditation, kept in the name Yogoda Satsanga Society of India.
Bengali for mad. Used by Tantrics and Bauls as a term of respect for a holy person who ignores convention, as in Bamakhepa.
A pilgrimage site where, in tradition, a part of the goddess Sati's body fell. Tarapith is counted among them.
A cremation ground. In Tantric practice it is a place for worship of the goddess because it holds what ordinary religion avoids.
The name of Ram, repeated aloud or silently as the central practice of Ram devotion.
Selfless service to others or to God, treated as worship.
Writing a mantra repeatedly in a notebook instead of speaking it.
Food offered to a deity or a teacher and then shared out as a blessing.
The fire offering at the heart of the sannyasa rite, in which the candidate symbolically gives his past life and desires to the fire before taking the ochre robe.
Group singing of divine names and short hymns, usually in call and response.
The period before dawn, traditionally about an hour and a half before sunrise, held to be the best time for prayer and meditation.

Sivananda's name for his method: one main path (service, devotion, knowledge or meditation) practised daily with smaller amounts of the others and some hatha yoga, so that head, heart and hand develop together.
In yogic and Ayurvedic physiology, a subtle vital essence said to be built up by conserving sexual energy; not a concept of modern medicine.

A sacred sound, syllable or phrase repeated aloud or silently. In Transcendental Meditation a short Sanskrit sound is given by the teacher and thought silently, with its meaning playing no part in the practice.
A ritual of worship or honour with offerings such as flowers, fruit, light and water. In TM a short puja to the line of masters ending with Brahmananda Saraswati precedes the giving of the mantra.
An extraordinary power said to come from advanced yoga practice; Patanjali's Yoga Sutras list many. The TM-Sidhi programme, spelled that way by the movement, is Maharishi's course built on them.
A seed mantra: a one-syllable sound such as aim or shrim used in Tantric and devotional practice, traditionally associated with a particular deity.
A celibate student devoted to a teacher or to sacred study; a stage before, or apart from, full monastic renunciation.
Literally installing the life breath; the temple rite that makes an image a living presence. Sadhguru uses it for his consecrations, such as the Dhyanalinga.
A seal or gesture; in yoga, a position of the body, hands or eyes held to direct attention or energy.
The first yogi; Sadhguru's name for Shiva as the source of yoga, presented as a teacher more than as a god to be worshipped.
Mark or sign; the rounded upright form in which Shiva is worshipped in temples.
The Bengal-centred devotional tradition founded on the teaching of Chaitanya (1486-1534), who is worshipped as Krishna in a combined form with Radha.
"Inconceivable oneness and difference." The Gaudiya view that souls are both one with and distinct from God, in a way reason cannot fully grasp.
"Marketplace of the name." Bhaktivinoda's network of local preaching centres built around kirtan and lectures.
A Vaishnava ascetic who has taken renunciant vows in a simple form, without joining an order of sannyasis.
The BAPS teaching that Swaminarayan is God (Purushottam) and that his eternal servant Akshar is present on earth as the guru, and that both are to be worshipped.
The collected discourses of Swaminarayan, recorded by his monks in 1819-1829, the central text of the Swaminarayan sect.
In Siddha Yoga and related kundalini teachings, an involuntary movement, sound, breath change or emotion said to arise when awakened kundalini purifies the body and mind.
Consciousness understood as an active, creative power, often addressed as a goddess; in Kashmir Shaivism the force through which Shiva manifests the world.
"I am That": a mantra linked with the natural breath, so on the in-breath and ham on the out-breath, affirming identity with the divine.
A Sanskrit hymn, attributed to the Skanda Purana, in which Shiva praises the guru as God; chanted daily in Siddha Yoga ashrams.

Inconceivable simultaneous oneness and difference: the Gaudiya Vaishnava teaching, systematised by Jiva Goswami, that souls and the world are one with God in quality and different from him in power, in a way beyond full understanding.

The great mantra: the sixteen-word Hare Krishna chant (Hare Krishna Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna Hare Hare, Hare Rama Hare Rama, Rama Rama Hare Hare), the central practice of Chaitanya's followers and ISKCON.
Congregational chanting of God's names, often in public with drums and cymbals; in ISKCON the word also covers book distribution as a form of preaching.
The third traditional stage of life, after student and householder, in which a person withdraws from family affairs before full renunciation.

Originally a Vedic officiating priest; in ISKCON, a representative who performs initiation on the guru's behalf. The ritvik movement holds that Prabhupada remains the initiating guru of all later members.
The guru's household: a traditional residential school where pupils live with their teacher. ISKCON's boarding schools used the name.
Doctrine of illusion: the name Vaishnava critics give to Advaita Vedanta, which they read as making the personal God and the individual soul finally unreal.
Instruction. A shiksha guru teaches and guides without necessarily giving formal initiation (diksha).
